imageCaption: The mofongo sits at the center of the dominoes table, the pressed morpho butterfly still resting on its golden surface, while the neighborhood gathers—some curious, some skeptical, all of them about to understand exactly who the Gomez family is.
text:
The potluck was happening in Marco's colmadón, which made sense because Marco's colmadón was the neighborhood's actual heart. The bodega was just the shape the heart had chosen.

Aaliyah was supposed to be nervous. She had the recipe for it—the heat climbing her throat, the way her hands wanted to be useful but there was nothing to do because the mofongo was already made, already blessed, already existing in a state of glitch-supported perfection that couldn't be improved by anything as mundane as worry.

Instead, she was watching the bowl sit at the center of the dominoes table like it was waiting to be auditioned for a very specific role in everyone's understanding of who they were.

"Stop vibrating," Elijah said from the chair next to her, which was his way of pointing out that anxiety looked a lot like enthusiasm and most people couldn't tell the difference if you moved fast enough.

"I'm not vibrating," Aaliyah said, vibrating slightly. "I'm maintaining structural integrity."

"That's vibrating," he confirmed. He had a snack—because Elijah always had a snack—and was working through it with the focus of someone who took nutrition very seriously even though that nutrition was invariably just whatever he could find. Today it appeared to be candied papaya. "The thing that helps is remembering that everyone here has already tasted something that shouldn't work. They've been living in a neighborhood where time takes coffee breaks. A recipe that doesn't make sense is going to feel like home."

Which was, aggravating, exactly right.

Sully barked once from under the table—contented, observational, the bark of a dog who understood that important social events should happen sitting down.

The dominoes crowd started arriving in that specific order that crowds have when they're curious but trying not to seem too eager. First came Mrs. Chen, who'd lived two buildings over for forty-three years and treated neighborhood events the way a general treated strategy—with attention and opinions. Then the twins from 4B, who were in the complicated age where they thought they were too cool for dominoes but not cool enough to stay home. Then a cascade of people who'd been watching the Gomez family settle into the yellow house with the specific attention reserved for situations that were definitely going to be interesting even if nobody was sure whether that interest should be cautious or delighted.

Marco brought the bowl forward with both hands, the way priests carried important things, and set it at the center of the dominoes table. The pressed morpho butterfly caught the light. Three people gasped.

"This," Marco announced, with the gravitas of a person who'd been waiting seventy-nine days to introduce something properly, "is what happens when a family that has spent two and a half months accidentally healing broken timelines decides to bring something to a neighborhood potluck."

Nobody moved toward it immediately. Which was fair. Mofongo that had been blessed by a temporal glitch while looking like it had been decorated with an impossible butterfly had earned the right to be approached with ceremony.

Mrs. Chen was the first, because Mrs. Chen was always first when something mattered. She picked up a small paper plate and moved forward like she was being pulled by something older than politeness. She took a generous spoonful. She ate it.

The sound she made wasn't a word. It was too complex for words. It was recognition and surprise and the specific feeling of tasting something you didn't know you'd been hungry for.

"Oh," she said, very quietly. "Oh my god."

That was all it took. Suddenly everyone was moving. The twins got in line behind Mrs. Chen. A woman Aaliyah didn't recognize stepped forward. A man with a very specific expression of skepticism picked up a plate and then tried the mofongo and then got a second plate because the first one couldn't possibly have been the right experience.

"They're understanding," Luisana said softly from the chair on Aaliyah's left. She had her journal out, naturally, recording the precise moment a neighborhood recognized what it had been waiting for. "They're understanding that you didn't make something traditional. You made something that tastes like movement and stillness at the same time. You made something that tastes like the choice to stop running."

"I made something that tastes like Dad putting random things on sale into a plane and seeing where they ended up," Aaliyah corrected. "I made something that tastes like you at 11:47 PM asking what it means to stay."

"Same thing," Luisana said, and wrote it down.

The mofongo was running out. People were getting thirds. Someone asked Marco for the recipe and when Marco pointed at Aaliyah, the whole gathering turned to look at her like she'd just walked out of a narrative nobody had the right to be living inside.

"Is it traditional?" one of the twins asked—not skeptically, genuinely curious.

"No," Aaliyah said, and then Anthony was there somehow, appearing with the specific Dad Energy that came from being proud of something his daughter had done. "It's traditional except where it's not. It's mofongo if mofongo had decided to take a spontaneous detour and ended up somewhere better."

"So like your vacation?" the other twin asked.

"Exactly like our vacation," Anthony confirmed. "Unplanned. Slightly illegal in terms of culinary tradition. Absolutely worth it."

And that was when Aaliyah felt it—the shift in the room, the moment when a neighborhood stops seeing a family as temporary and starts seeing them as someone who belongs. Not because they fit perfectly into the existing shape of things. But because they'd arrived with something genuine and weird and delicious, and they'd offered it up and let the neighborhood decide what to do with it.

The morpho butterfly was still sitting on top of the empty bowl, having been carefully moved aside by people taking their portions. Abuela Ida, probably, taking attendance. Making sure her granddaughter understood that some recipes changed things because they were made by someone who believed they mattered.

"Day eighty," Luisana whispered, writing. "The day the neighborhood said yes."

And Aaliyah realized, watching Mrs. Chen ask Anthony for his contact information—not as a courtesy but like she was making sure he knew he wasn't allowed to leave—that the potluck wasn't the ending of something.

It was the beginning of something. The beginning of a family that had healed the world realizing they could also feed it.

One mofongo at a time.
